composition.story: A transformer never reads words directly. It splits the sentence into tokens, turns each token into an ID, and uses the ID to pick one row of a learned table. Then it adds a position vector. Follow "the cat saw the dog": the repeated word "the" starts identical but ends up different.

aha.observation: Both 'the' tokens copy the same table row, but adding different position vectors gives them different input embeddings.

controls.label: Step
controls.presentation: Previous / Next buttons; the step rail shows the current state

controls.label: Embedding size
controls.presentation: Selects the variant. It changes the table size and the vector length in the readouts.

controls.label: Reset
controls.presentation: Returns to step 1 and the toy size

states.label: Sentence
states.sentence: The input is five words. The word 'the' appears twice, at positions 0 and 3.
states.why: Text is not numbers, so the model must convert each word.

states.label: Split into tokens
states.sentence: A tokenizer cuts the text into tokens. Here each word is one token, so there are five.
states.why: Tokens are the units the model's vocabulary knows.

states.label: Tokens to IDs
states.sentence: Each token is looked up in the vocabulary and becomes an integer ID. Both 'the' tokens get ID 0.
states.why: An ID is only a row number, with no meaning yet.

states.label: Pick table rows
states.sentence: Each ID selects one row of the learned table E. Row 0 is copied for both 'the' tokens.
states.why: Training tunes the table values. Lookup only copies a row.

states.label: Make position vectors
states.sentence: The row says nothing about word order. So each position gets its own vector, PE(pos), from sines and cosines.
states.why: Position 0 and position 3 get different vectors.

states.label: Add: input embeddings
states.sentence: Input x_i = E[id_i] + PE(i). Both 'the' tokens start from E[0] but end with different vectors.
states.why: The same word is now told apart by where it sits.
